en: The *Kālacakrāvatāra* by the venerable scholar Abhayākaragupta. Oṃ! Homage to Mañjuśrī!

I bow to my own Jaina self, which is accessible to all people, which possesses a body that is formless yet consists of form and other qualities, whose nature is beyond conceptualization, which assumes a universal form, and which bestows boundless bliss through the non-duality of wisdom and compassion.
Those stars which bestow beauty upon the sky and announce both prosperity and calamity, shining as if within the heart of the Tathāgata, now triumph over the darkness.

For here, indeed, because the heterodox teachers (tīrthika), afflicted by stinginess, have concealed the established doctrine (siddhānta) regarding astronomy, even though they have composed an elaborate *laghukaraṇa*, it is not understood nowadays; therefore, that [doctrine] is now set forth. When a year begins with the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) of the month of Caitra, one should write four hundred and sixty-three [units], and then this [value] should be combined with that.
That [number], diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, becomes the pure annual constant (*varṣadhruvaka*). Multiplied by twelve, it is the lunar-month aggregate (*māsapiṇḍa*).

When the months begin with Caitra and end with Āmāvāsya (the new moon), that [aggregate] is added [to the year]; having placed it in two positions, the lower one is multiplied by four and divided by one thousand three hundred and twenty; the remainder of the division is to be discarded.
When [the breath] has been attained and has entered the head, the head becomes a pure mass of months;
however, when she is two years old, a year must be calculated as thirteen months, and two months should be counted as one,
and the entry into the month of Caitra should not be performed.

Having added that pure *māsapiṇḍa* to the three places, it is multiplied by the "hand-fire" (thirty-two). From the middle place, one subtracts the quotient obtained from the lower place divided by six;
if there is a remainder, one must also subtract from that the quotient obtained by dividing by six.
Here, from the lower place increased by thirty, one subtracts the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty, and adds this result to the top place increased by two.
The remainder of the division shall be the aggregate of the rods;
the remainder of seven divisions at the head shall be the aggregate of the days;
however, nothing is obtained [in this case].

Again, having placed the pure accumulated months mixed with one hundred and twelve in two places, the remainder from the division by six in the lower position shall be the component of the *piṇḍa*. The quotient obtained from the division, increased by five and doubled in the upper position, should be added [to the lower].
Then, from the upper value divided by twenty-eight, the remainder of the division shall be the *pada-piṇḍa*.
Here, the sequence of the weekday-piṇḍa, the daṇḍa-piṇḍa, the pada-piṇḍa, and the components of the piṇḍa should be written down one below the other.

Furthermore, in the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṅgraha*, regarding the pure months situated in the three positions, [the value] is multiplied by the lords of the middle positions; from the result, forty-nine is subtracted. Having divided by sixty the quotient obtained from the subtraction, the remainder of the division is to be known as the *ghaṭī* of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
The quotient, however, having been doubled, should be added to the top [value].
Then, the sum of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra-piṇḍa) remaining after dividing the [total] by twenty-seven should be known from the head [of the calculation].

Here, below the sum of the lunar mansions, the sum of the lunar mansion-hours (ṛkṣa-ghaṭī-piṇḍa) should be written. This occurs when neither the year is entered into the annual zodiacal sign (varṣa-rāśi) nor the month is entered into the sum of the pure months (śuddha-māsa-piṇḍa).

Then, month by month, one, thirty-two, two, and one should be added respectively to the weekday, the *daṇḍa*, the *pada*, and the *piṇḍāvayava*; two *ghaṭīs* and eleven (*rudra*) should be added to the asterism;
and at the commencement of a new year, a different set of weekday-piṇḍas and so forth must be calculated.

For the purpose of determining the weekday and the duration of the lunar day (*tithi*) each day, the elapsed and current lunar days of the present month, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), are to be added or subtracted respectively into the *vāra*, *nāḍī*, and *pada* values; or, if the quotient obtained by dividing the total sum (*piṇḍa*) by fourteen is two or four, or if no such quotient is obtained, the *piṇḍa* itself is to be added as an equal value.
When one or three [of these] are obtained, it is uneven; beyond this there is no further division,
because a total (piṇḍa) is not obtained above twenty-seven.

Divide by twenty-eight; those [results] together with thirty lunar days (tithis) do not exceed fifty-seven. When the [resulting] lunar stations (candrapada) are even, they are to be added; when odd, they are to be subtracted. However, if the remainder of the division is zero, [the correction] is zero. In the case of the lunar station of the thirty-three and the moon (tridaśaśaśipada), it is purified; in the case of the five-eyed and the sun (pañcanetrārkaka), it is ten; in the case of the lunar station of the ten oceans (daśajaladhipada), it is twenty less one. In the case of the one called the lunar day (tithi), it is eleven; in the case of fire (agni), it is ten. In the case of the lunar station of the four oceans (caturjaladhipada), it is twenty. In the case of the one less than that, it is nineteen.

In the twenty-second and fifth lunar days, there are twenty-two and eighteen [units] respectively; in the seventh, twenty-five. In that [seventh], all the solar [units] manifested through the divisions of the signs are to be added or subtracted.
Since it is pure, there is nothing therein to be given or abandoned; thus, within that mass of the pot,
the solar positions arise through the differentiation of the sun.

If the Sun’s debt is in that [total], it is a debt for the Sun; if the Sun’s wealth is in that, it is wealth for the Sun—this is the differentiation of the Sun. This has been stated: having added the quotient obtained from the division by the elements and so forth according to the method to be explained, and having subtracted as many solar-motion steps as there are, the result is called the "Sun’s Shadow" (*ravikā*). If the entry of Kālacakra occurs during the Sun’s enjoyment, then it should be added to the day-counters (*vāraghaṭī*).
Now, that which is to be subtracted from the solar longitude is likewise to be subtracted from this [lunar longitude];
thus, for the Moon’s purification, there are two [sets of] solar values: the lunar-solar values and the lunar-pada values, which are 4, 25, 10, and 1, in the eastern and western halves respectively.

(Kā0 Taṃ0 1.32) Having drawn a vertical line in the eastern part in ascending order and a horizontal line in the middle, one should write [the names] in the western part from bottom to top in reverse order, such as Śaśin and so forth; thus, there are exactly fourteen [squares], which is the placement of the positions for all the planets.

Regarding the term *pada*: here, the *sañcārapada* (the station of movement) is established for all planets as consisting of *ghaṭikās* (units of time), determined by the remainder of the fourteen parts; the movement (*sañcāra*) occurs above that, wherein the planet has entered.
Having multiplied that by the divisor, divide by one hundred and twenty-six;
the quotient is the elapsed *pada* in the first half,
while in the second half, having subtracted that, the unelapsed *pada* itself is to be added to or subtracted from the place of the *ghaṭikās* of the weekday.
However, in this world, the *ravikās* are impure; therefore, for the sake of obtaining a pure *ravikā*,
one establishes the weekday starting from one and so forth in the place of the day,
and the *daṇḍas* and so forth in the lunar date (*tithi*), which are to be experienced starting from sunrise.

For the purpose of determining the Sun’s daily transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), one should take the lunar day (*tithi*) stated for the beginning of the bright fortnight and place it in two locations. In one location, multiply it by four *daṇḍas*; in the other, multiply it by twenty, twenty-two, or twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s according to the method of the *Karaṇas* or the method of the *Siddhāntas*. Then, having multiplied [the result] by sixty, add the quotient to the upper [value]. Furthermore, having multiplied the upper *daṇḍas* by sixty, add the quotient to the *ṛkṣa* (mansions); the remainder of the division is added to the *ṛkṣa-daṇḍas*, and the *pāṇīpala*s should be written below the *ṛkṣa-daṇḍas*.

When the asterism, its duration in daṇḍas, its total duration in palas, and the hand-measures are placed in two locations, one should subtract six asterisms—starting from Aśvinī and including Meṣa—for the sake of determining the Sun's position at three signs;
the asterism thus subtracted becomes the next immediate birth-sign.

As it is said: "In Meṣa and Yugma (Vṛṣabha), [the lords are] Candra, Śukra, and Ravi; in Siṃha, Kanyā, and Tulā, Bhauma, Mantrī (Guru), and Rāhu; and in Vṛścika, Antya (Dhanus), and Cāpa, Budha, Śani, and Phaṇin (Rāhu)."
In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṅgraha*, regarding the phrase "beginning and end" (*ādyanta*),
it is stated that Saturn (*śauri*) is at the beginning of the bow (*cāpa*) and Ketu is at the end.

Here, if the debt (*ṛṇa*) is greater than the remaining portion of the zodiacal sign (*bhogarāśi*), then it should be subtracted after adding it to the position of the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣasthāna*) within the cycle of twenty-seven constellations (*saptaviṃśati-nakṣatra-cakra*).
If the remainder after subtraction should be half the circle (*cakrārddha*), then that half-circle must be subtracted; in that case alone is it to be known as *utkrama* (inverse order).
When the half-circle has not been subtracted, it is simply *krama* (direct order).

From the *ṛkṣas* (nakṣatras) multiplied by sixty and joined with the *ghaṭikās* situated below, the quotient obtained by dividing by fifteen (the elements, fires, and moon) is to be subtracted; having thus determined the *rāśicaraṇa* (zodiacal step), there are six zodiacal steps (*ṣaḍrāśipadāni*) for the slow motion (*mandakārya*) in the six signs beginning with Cancer as the birth sign. These same steps apply to all planets in their slow motion. However, when no quotient is obtained by division by fifteen and so forth, it should be understood everywhere that the planet is in the first movement-step (*prathamacārapada*).
Then, the operation to be described beginning with "by that, others are multiplied" and so forth should be performed;
likewise, in the slow motion (*mandakārya*), for all planets, a debt (*ṛṇa*) is to be understood by direct order (*krama*) and a credit (*dhana*) by reverse order (*utkrama*).
Thereafter, the second *pada* from the traversed *pada* is being traversed; this is the "motion" (*bhoga*) here.

From the remaining *nāḍīs* after being divided by that [number], the degrees traversed by the planet according to the sign in the first half [of the circle] are summed together with the portion of the enjoyment of the *bhūtādi* (elemental) divisions. However, in the second half, having subtracted the portion of enjoyment obtained by division, the untraversed degrees and positions are summed together with the other portion of enjoyment; these are to be added or subtracted according to whether they constitute a credit (*dhana*) or a debt (*ṛṇa*). Or rather, this same [calculation] regarding the *nāḍīs* of the planet's movement constitutes the "pure sun" (*śuddharavikā*) for the sun; thus, in the place of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the asterism and so forth traversed, the remainder of what has been traversed, and what is yet to be traversed are determined.
This same rule applies to the moon and to the conjunction (*yoga*) as well, which will be explained later.
Now the impure solar days (*ravika*) of the Sun are stated: Time (1), taste (6), and indeed *hi* (2); ten, Hara (3), Hara (3), Rudra (11), direction (10), and six.

At the end of the northern course (ayana), fire (vahni) and ether (kha) become wealth (dhanam) and debt (ṛṇam) respectively in the north and south; the sun moves for six months through the divisions of fortnights due to the distinctions of monthly transits (saṅkrānti).
Here, in Cancer and so forth, time (kāla) is the first fortnight as debt, while in the second [fortnight] it is the essence (rasa) of Cancer.
In this manner, up until the end of the [northern] solstice (*ayana*), fire (*vahni*) and space (*kha*) are added to the bow (*dhanus*);
likewise, from Capricorn (*makara*) onwards, it is a debt (*dhana*).

For the purpose of calculating the Moon’s transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the lunar days (*tithi*) stated for the bright fortnight (*śukla*) and so forth should be added to the solar transit at the position of the lunar mansion.

Thereafter, those lunar days (tithis), multiplied by six (rasa) and placed in another position, are mixed with the elapsed ghaṭīs and so forth of the weekday according to the *Kālacakra* system; this is to be known as a subtraction from the ghaṭī-position of the sun,
whereby the lunar motion (candrabhoga) shall result.

The lunar day (tithi) beginning from the bright fortnight is calculated here by means of the sun’s motion; when these [calculated days] are reduced by one, provided such is possible, the remainder after division by seven shall be the *karaṇa*.
The *karaṇa* is not a separate motion; it is simply the motion of the lunar day itself.
Here, the general rule is that the breaths which do not remain above the place of the breath enter into the *pāṇīpala*s as the quotient obtained by dividing by six.
Those [units] also do not remain above sixty;
the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty enters into the *ghaṭīs*,
and the *ghaṭīs* likewise enter into the weekday or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Even the days of the week, having been seven, perish;
even the twenty-seven lunar mansions here do not remain forever;
and the same is true for the yogas.

Likewise, there is one constellation consisting of sixty *daṇḍas*, as well as the day of the week (*vāra*), the conjunction (*yoga*), and the day (*dina*); therein, the days of the week are seven, beginning with Āditya,
and the lunar dates (*tithi*) are fifteen, beginning with the first day (*pratipad*).

The twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī. Likewise, the [twenty-seven] lunar yogas (*yoga*) are: Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarmā, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, and so forth.
The twenty-seven *karaṇas* are: Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti;
and the seven [others] are: Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi;
likewise, there are eleven [more]: Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna.

In this regard, beginning from the latter half of the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, the enjoyment of each [deity] for four watches (*prahara*) should be understood by repeating them in sequence until the first half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; this constitutes the enjoyment of the seven [deities].

Then, beginning from the latter half of that same day until the first half of the first lunar day of the bright fortnight, the enjoyment of the other four [deities] occurs; here, having divided the duration of each lunar day into two equal parts, the distinction between the first and second halves is to be known.
The sequence of the fivefold calendar (pañcāṅga)—consisting of the day of the week, lunar date, asterism (nakṣatra), yoga, and karaṇ—is as follows:
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and one quarter of Kṛttikā constitute Aries.

In this manner, each sign is formed by nine quarters; thus, the twelve zodiac signs—Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—are to be understood as occurring in the months beginning with Vaiśākha.

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṅgraha*, Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Sun; Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter are recognized as the lords of the fields (*kṣetriṇaḥ*) in these signs respectively. Thus it is said.
The pure years (śuddhavarṣāṇi),

which are the pure years (śuddhābdā) increased by eight, are multiplied by four hundred; these are then diminished by the pure years increased by eight separately, and the result divided by three hundred seventeen, with two added, yields the days of the week (vārāḥ).
Multiply the remaining degrees by sixty and convert them into *nāḍīs*; divide by seven and take the quotient; the remainder is discarded.
To the obtained *ghaṭīs* add thirty, divide by sixty, and take the quotient; add two to the weekday and take the remainder by twenty.
These are the *vāra-ghaṭikās*, which form the constant (*dhruvaka*) below.

The fixed weekday for the solar transit (saṅkrānti) at the end of the year shall be the remainder after dividing by seven; above that [value], it should be added. Here, when the Sun leaves Pisces and enters Aries, twelve are added; these are the additive values (kṣepaka) for Aries and the subsequent signs in order: 14, 72, 53, 19, 17, and 18 in the third [sign].

In the first [house], four, three, and one; in the second, two, one, and two; in the third, four, two, and three; in the fourth, six, one, and two; in the fifth, five and one; in the sixth, six and one; and in the seventh, five, one, seven, three, six, one, four, seven, and three.
"Six, two, zero, zero; eyes, arrows, and a quarter [in the sign] of Pisces for the Sun.

Thus (Kālacakra-tantra 1.37–38). This is their arrangement: among these twelve compartments, the first [value]—the *vāradhuva* (weekday constant)—is to be added to each [compartment] as the planetary *ghaṭī*; the second [value], beginning with fifty-seven, is to be added to the *ghaṭīdhuva* (hour constant).
Thus, the transits (saṅkrānti) and their durations for the weekdays are to be known from the Karaṇa.
Now, for the purpose of determining the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) duration of Mars and the others, the calculation of the day-count (ahargaṇa) is stated:

having multiplied the pure months by thirty for the sake of the heap of days, and having added the lunar days (tithis) as stated starting from the bright fortnight (śukla), one places them in three positions; then, having divided the lower heap by 703, the quotient is to be added to the middle [heap].
Then, the upper heap [of days] diminished by the quotient obtained from dividing the middle heap by sixty-four shall be the uncorrected day-count (*asphuṭa-dinagaṇa*).

Having placed that in two positions, one is divided by seven; if the weekday for that day does not coincide, then one or other units should be added to or subtracted from the first heap so that it corresponds to the correct weekday.
Thereafter, the corrected day-count (*sphuṭa-ahargaṇa*) is obtained.

For the purpose of determining the [mean] Mars, from the *ahargaṇa* increased by one hundred and sixty-seven, one should divide by the days of Mars’s mandala—namely, 257—and the quotient representing completed zodiacal revolutions is to be discarded. The same applies to the others. From the remainder, multiplied by the asterism (nakṣatra), one divides by the days of its own mandala; the quotient is the asterism above. From that remainder, multiplied by sixty, one divides by the days of its own mandala; the quotient is the *nāḍīs* below, and the *pāṇīpalas* and so forth are as before. Having placed this result, beginning with the asterism, in two places, one should subtract nine and a half asterisms from one of them.
Thereafter, the previously stated [positions] for the Sun, such as Aries and Aśvinī, are to be understood; however,

for one situated in the specific [calculation], the eighteen principles (*tattva*) and mountains (*adri*) are the *pada*s in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*), which are to be added to or subtracted from the other [longitude] starting from the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) and so forth.
Thus is the purification for the slow motion (*mandakarma*) in the case of Mars.

However, in the case of the fast motion (*śīghrakarma*), one should place the purified degrees of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—purified according to the slow motion—in two places. One [set] is to be subtracted from the solar longitude (the Sun's position) as corrected by the Sun, when mixed with the lunar days (*tithi*) and not yet subtracted, provided the procedure for discarding six asterisms plus three quarters has not been performed.
Thereafter, the sequence beginning with "if it is a debt, as stated for the Sun" and ending with "in this very order" is to be understood.

In this matter of swift calculation, wealth (addition) should be applied in direct order and debt (subtraction) in reverse order. Having determined the quotient obtained from the remainder—which is the "pada" (step) indicating the planetary movement after subtracting as much as possible—one should discard it. Then, having multiplied that remainder by sixty *nāḍīs* with that same *pada*, the result obtained by dividing by sixty should be combined with a portion of that *pada*. In the first half [of the calculation], the accumulated *caraṇas* (steps) traversed by the planet according to the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) are thus established.

In the latter half, however, having subtracted the quotient obtained from that [half] as a portion of the term, those unexpired [days] along with the other portion of that term are to be added elsewhere to the planetary longitude once the slow-motion correction has been purified; or rather, those fourteen terms which are here in the *Laghugranthasaṅgraha* of the *Kālacakra Tantra*: "The Victor, three, fire, eye, variety, hand, twice-eight, eighteen, day, Śiva, and fire from the root."
Eleven, three, fire (three), sky (zero), serpent (eight), and earth (one)—these are the fivefold [digits] of Mars.

From the root [of the center], along the horizontal middle line, the steps for the swift calculation of Jupiter are: eight, six, six, two; then from the root of each direction, three, six, nine, eleven, eleven, and seven.
The steps of Saturn are 64, 52, 40, 32, 20, 16, 8, and 3.
Likewise, having placed the half-verse concerning the slow Sun (manda-sūrya) in two locations, one should subtract it from both the motion of Mercury and the motion of Venus.

Then, having performed the procedure immediately following that— starting from "of the subtracted [quantity]" and ending with "the untraversed portions" (*abhuktāni*) as stated for Mars— one should apply [those values] as additions or subtractions to the other slow Sun.
In this very manner, the period of Mercury and the period of Venus also become kings. From that king, [the periods are] the lunar day (tithi), then the mind (manu), the limbs (aṅga), Śiva (eleven),
the mountains (seven), five (pañcama), from the root (mūla) the lords of the waters (four), twenty, and twenty-eight.
For the gentle [Mercury], thirty-four; for the Jinas [Buddhas], three principles, two, and twice two;
for the eyes, defects, and lunar days, eight; from the Mūla [nakṣatra], six, zero, and fire;
then the cavities, cavities, qualities, and mountains—these are the steps for Venus during its swift motion.
Thus ends the purification of the swift motion (*śīghrakarma*) for Mars and the other planets.

For the purpose of purifying Mercury in its slow motion (*mandakarma*), one should perform the calculation starting from "the clear day-count multiplied by one hundred" and ending with "the result in *pāṇīpala* and so forth," as was done for Mars. This [result], beginning with the asterism (*nakṣatra*) and so on, is stated as the course (*cāra*) for the sake of the swift motion.

Therefore, for that purpose, having established it in another place and having placed it in two locations—one being the Sun's longitude free from the *ravikāra* correction—one should subtract sixteen and a half lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) from the Sun's longitude there.

Then, having applied the corrections stated for the Sun—beginning with "Aries" and ending with "according to the nature of debt or credit"—those [results] should be added to the other Sun's longitude;
thus, Mercury is purified in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakarma*).

*The Introduction to Kālacakra*: This other solar motion, having attained the nature of Mercury purified by the slow [mean] operation, is called the "slow sun" for the purpose of the fast [true] operation.
For the slow calculation, there are one thousand seven hundred and ten steps.

For the purpose of purifying Jupiter, one should subtract twenty-six hundred and forty from the group of days of the true [mean] sun; then, dividing by the days of Jupiter’s revolution—four thousand three hundred and thirty-two—one obtains [the result], and so forth; the calculation is to be performed as with Mars.
In this regard, the specific detail is as follows:

the twelve asterisms to be subtracted and the nine steps of Hari and Śikhin for the sake of Venus' purification should be performed entirely like Mercury, starting from the clear day-count (*ahargaṇa*) reduced by ten and diminished by eighty-four, with the quotient obtained by dividing by the days of Venus' orbit— 725— and so forth.
But this is the distinction: six asterisms are to be subtracted, and the pādas are five, two, and one.

For the sake of purifying Saturn, one should perform the calculation starting with "the quotient obtained by dividing the clear ahargaṇa diminished by eighty-four thousand four hundred and four by the days of Saturn’s revolution, which are sixty-six thousand three hundred and forty-one," and so forth, as in the case of Mars. The specific difference, however, is that eighteen asterisms, twenty-two, fifteen, and four are to be subtracted; this is the purification for Mercury and the others in their slow-motion (manda) operation.

Moreover, the experts in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) maintain that when the planetary motion purified by the slow motion (*mandakarma*) is purified by the fast motion (*śīghrakarma*), the planetary position becomes purified by both motions; it is not the case that the position purified by the slow motion is one thing and the one purified by the fast motion is another. Furthermore, the positions purified by both motions belong only to Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn; for the Sun, [the correction] is by the slow motion alone, and for the Moon, by the fast motion alone.

For the purpose of calculating Rāhu’s transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), one should take the pure months, add two and twelve to them, and double that total for the purpose of determining the sign (*rāśi*) of the fortnight (*pakṣa*). For a solar eclipse on the full moon, one adds one fortnight; for a solar eclipse on the new moon, one adds two fortnights. From these, the portion obtained by dividing by the *pakṣa-maṇḍala* of Rāhu—namely, 4062—is to be subtracted. From the remaining fortnights, multiplied by twenty-seven, the portion obtained by dividing by ten thousand is the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*).
From the remaining [values] multiplied by sixty, the ghaṭīs are obtained by division by [the sequence starting with] zero;
from their remainders likewise, the liptās;
and the remainders of those, multiplied by sixty and divided by [the same sequence starting with] zero, yield the śvāsas (breaths).
By means of these obtained asterisms and so forth, the twenty-seven asterisms constitute the mouth-bhoga (mouth-enjoyment) of Rāhu;
that same mouth-bhoga, when mixed with thirteen and a half asterisms, becomes the tail-bhoga (tail-enjoyment).
Thereafter, in the solar bhoga for each month, there are two asterisms and eleven ghaṭikās; over six months, this amounts to twelve asterisms and sixty-six ghaṭikās.
And those [fortnights] become thirteen, totaling fifty-three.
Here, in the solar longitude, at the time of a solar eclipse during the conjunction of the new moon, the *ravikās* are to be added or subtracted;
then, from the lunar node (*rāhu*)'s longitude, one should subtract forty-five *ghaṭikās*, thereby clearing away the remainder of the asterism's longitude (*nakṣatrabhoga*).
In that regard, if the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) should be equal [in longitude] to either the mouth or the tail,

only then— according to the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṅgraha*— is there an eclipse, and not otherwise; or else, having calculated the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) by the previously mentioned method, one should subtract the solar longitude from the longitude of Rāhu’s mouth or his tail.
During a lunar eclipse on the full moon day, one should subtract the Moon’s longitude from Rāhu’s mouth or Rāhu’s tail;
there is an eclipse when the Moon is in the same asterism as either the mouth or the tail, and not otherwise.
For here, at the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*)—either at the end of the new moon or the end of the full moon—the orbs of the Sun and Moon enter the orb of Rāhu.

Regarding the term *maṇḍala* [derived from the word *śabda*]: sixty *nāḍikās* constitute the transit of one lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and that should be understood as consisting of twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and sixteen digits (*kalā*). In that regard, if the transit of these two is subtracted from the transit of Rāhu, then there is a total eclipse lasting for the full duration of sixty *nāḍikās*; if half the transit is subtracted, there is a partial eclipse.
The conjunction of the planets is to be known as occurring until the fourth part of the *kalā*— which consists of four *nāḍīs*— has entered Rāhu’s orbit;
and when Rāhu swallows [the planet] in its mouth-orbit, it is the eastern portion, whereas in its tail-orbit, it is the western portion.
In this way, the movement [of the shadow] toward the other cardinal and intermediate directions is to be understood; thus says the commentary.
Furthermore, this eclipse occurs precisely after six months. In ultimate reality, Rāhu, whose nature is darkness, swallows only the moon because it possesses cool rays, not the sun.
However, at the time when the moon has entered the sun at the end of the new moon (amāvāsyā), there is the conventional expression that "he swallows the sun."
Thus is the purification of Rāhu.

Ketu, having entered the solar disc, moves daily for four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *liptās* along with the motion of the Sun; it moves two and a half *liptās* [further] during its swift motion (*śīghracāra*), proceeding forward in regular order (*krama*) and behind in reverse order (*utkrama*) during its retrograde motion (*vakracāra*).
Having remained thus for three years, it emerges.
Having emerged, it rises every day for two *ghaṭīs*—
a *ghaṭī* being fifty-six and a quarter *liptās* in duration— and for one month it appears like a star without smoke; thereafter, for one fortnight, the comet becomes manifest.
Thus, at the end of one and a half months, it again becomes invisible within the solar disc in the same manner for a period of three years;
its first appearance should be understood by observing what is well-known.
In this way, its appearance is known once in an infinite amount of time—this is the purification of Ketu.

In this regard, the general rule is as follows: for a planet that has risen from the solar disc during its direct motion (*kramagamana*) in a fast movement (*śīghrakarman*), the occupation (*bhoga*) in the first half of the fourteen *caraṇa*-units of time is said to be fast motion (*śīghracāra*),
while the occupation in the latter half is slow motion (*mandacāra*).
Then, when half the circle has been relinquished, there is a transgression of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*);
in the first half, it is called "retrograde motion" (*vakra-cāra*), and in the second half, "emergent motion" (*nirgama-cāra*),
due to the abandonment of the circle of zodiac signs and lunar mansions.

In this sequence, according to the rule, regarding the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) to be established: the "emergence of the planets" (*grahotkrama*)—the descent of the *vakra* (retrograde) Kālacakra—is as follows: in the first half [of the month], there is an increase of wealth and the planets face east;
in the second half, there is a loss of wealth and they face south.
In the reverse sequence (*utkrama*), in the first half, there is an increase of debt and they face west.

In the latter half [of the month], there is a loss of debt for those facing north; for these others, facing other directions occurs due to the influence of portents (*ariṣṭa*) and so forth. By nature, however, Rāhu faces west and circumambulates Meru clockwise, while the other planets face east; consequently, because it is obscured by the rays of the sun, the sun undergoes setting.
There is no total absence of the planet;

rather, its rising occurs here in this world in that very same manner. By virtue of the increase and decrease in the solar and lunar movements within the domain [of the earth], there is an increase of ten *nāḍīs* during the day and a decrease at night, derived from a tenth part of the sixty-*nāḍī* nature of the day-and-night (*ahorātra*).

From the boundary of the Southern Fire-circle (*dakṣiṇāgni-valaya*) up to the boundary of the Great Snow-circle (*mahāhima-valaya*), there is a northward course (*uttarāyaṇa*) for six months, covering seventy-five thousand *yojanas*.

Thus, from the boundary of the Great Himavat circle up to the boundary of the Southern Fire circle, during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana), there is an increase in the night and a decrease in the day.
This being so, it should be understood that there is a decrease or increase of two *liptās* every day and night.

Likewise, from the regions of Bhota, Līca, China, and so forth, up to the land of Sambhala, there is a decrease or increase of three *nāḍīs* obtained by dividing [the distance] into nine, eight, or seven parts; in the region of Kailāśa, it is by six parts. From the region of Kailāśa to the north, up to the Snowy Mountain (Himagiri), there is a decrease or increase of three *liptās* plus four breaths (*śvāsa*) every day and night.
Outside the Himālaya, in the eight directions, there is a single sphere of the constellations and zodiac signs in the form of a circle; in its center is the equatorial line (viṣuvarekhā),
and for this very reason, on both sides it takes the shape of a bow.
And here, like a donkey in the midst of a threshing floor or like a bull wandering about, the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī and ending with half of Citrā revolve along the northern line;

whereas those beginning with the other half of Citrā and ending with Revatī revolve on the southern side. Within these very [mansions], two and a quarter lunar mansions constitute one zodiac sign (*rāśi*).
In this manner, there are twelve zodiac signs, and the planets are their consumers.

And of this globe, during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), its northern extremity proceeds from the beginning of the northern circle of fire (*vahnivalaya*) and its southern extremity touches the southern limit of the Snowy Mountain (*himagiri*);
whereas during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), its southern extremity proceeds from the beginning of the southern circle of fire.
The northern extremity, however, touches the northern limit of the Snowy Mountains;
and these constellations and other celestial bodies, by virtue of their revolving clockwise around Sumeru, form a spherical shape.
The measurement of this sphere extends from the Southern Fire-Circle to the Great Himavat Mountains, being five thousand seven hundred and thirty *yojanas*.
From these [mandala-dinas], the sun relinquishes daily a directional division obtained by dividing [the total] by one hundred and eighty-two and a half;

thus, the transverse course of the sun across the twelve sectors is to be understood—this is the method of calculation (karaṇamārga). However, even by this method of calculation, there is no constant accuracy regarding the sun.

Just as in the case of day and night—there being no "three" in the eight directions and no "daily"—in this *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṅgraha*, when the solar motion is impure, Mars and the other planets, though corrected, do not become clear here; they are like trees whose roots have perished. Therefore, the path of the Siddhānta is now stated.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:
on level ground, one should place a gnomon measuring two *vitastis* at the center of a circular mandala measuring one cubit in diameter.

When the shadow of the gnomon in the forenoon, gradually contracting from outside the lines, enters the central point of the line on the edge of the mandala, then a mark in the shape of a crow’s foot (*kākapada*) should be made at that spot; that very direction is the west.
In the afternoon, as she gradually proceeds from the center of the mandala, one should mark the signs as before with the words "when she arrives" and so forth. That very direction is the east.

Here, having held the thread over a single sign and reaching up to the other sign, one should draw the mandala with chalk; then, having held the thread over the other sign, one should likewise act so that it forms the shape of a fish.
The direction of the south is the middle of the mouth of the fish situated between those two circles, and the direction of the north is the middle of its tail;

having thus determined the directions and erased these two circles, one should perform the examination at midday, beginning from the tenth day prior to the day of the sun’s northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*).

In that regard, first, from the center of the northern boundary line of the mandala, one enters the center of the mandala on whichever day that is the day of the sun’s transit into the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa-saṅkrānti*). On that day—with its specific weekday (*vāra*), lunar date (*tithi*), yoga, and karaṇa—the solar longitude (*sūryabhoga*) is the fundamental constant (*mūladhruvaka*): twenty in the place of the asterisms (*nakṣatra-sthāna*) and fifteen in the place of the *ghaṭikās*, calculated by adding nine months starting from Vaiśākha and nine zodiac signs starting from Aries.

In that fixed calculation (*dhruvaka*), one should add four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s every day and subtract the solar steps (*ravikāpada*) according to the previously mentioned method, beginning with "six constellations and three-quarters are to be subtracted," and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Mūlatantra*: "From the commencement of the solstice (*ayana*), [the correction] should be added daily until another solstice occurs."
"The station of the sky (the ether) should be purified according to the prescribed ritual procedure for karma.

Thus, the results of the transitions of the planets regarding the days of the week, lunar dates, asterisms, yogas, karaṇas, zodiac signs, and fields are easily understood from other sources; therefore, they are not elaborated upon here.

This *udāna* has arisen from the Tree; this light is its fruit, for it is not yet renowned here. Having descended into the *Kālacakra*, may that one of excellent intellect, through the descent into *Kālacakra*, easily effect the unimpeded arrangement of words. May the composition of Abhaya extend the path of discernment to the heart; may the great-souled ones forgive [any faults] in what has been composed here.

May the merit [of this work] shine forth most brightly, and may the wealth of the Victors bear fruit throughout the three worlds. Thus ends the *Kālacakrāvatāra*. This is the composition of the venerable scholar Abhayākaragupta. Now, regarding the movements: the Moon traverses one zodiac sign every month; the Sun traverses one zodiac sign every thirteen days; and [the following are] the number of days for the orbs of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.

In the Siddhānta, the days of the solar mandala are [365]; the daily allotment is 1 daṇḍa and 1 pāṇīpala. For the Moon, the days of the mandala are 29; the daily allotment is 1 daṇḍa and 1 pāda. For Rāhu, the day is one tithi; the allotment is 1 pāda and half a śvāsa. For Mars, it is 1 daṇḍa and 1 pāda and half a śvāsa. For Mercury, it is 1 pāda. For Jupiter, it is 1 pāda and half a śvāsa. For Venus, it is half a śvāsa. For Saturn, it is 1 pāda. These are the daily daṇḍas and pādas. From the Sun, there is an excess of two and a half liptās per day. The Śaka years [are calculated] from the Śaka year... by dividing by sixty...
...originating from... for the purpose of carrying [the fire], just as in this manner...
it was not written by the venerable Śrīmitra...
having mixed with Rudra... Vyā...
The Year, the Years beginning with Prabhava, and the Introduction to the Glorious Kālacakra— by the Master and Great Paṇḍita...
